newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban exploit anti-Dostum revolt in north.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban exploit anti-Dostum revolt in north.

text.p: A revolt against General Abdul Rashid Dostum has given Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia a new chance to defeat its opponents and impose its rule throughout a land wasted by decades of war.
Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, is facing a deadly challenge from a mutinous general, Abdul Malik, who launched an uprising in the north on Monday, apparently in collusion with the Taleban.

The Taleban, who captured Kabul in September and already control all but a few northern provinces, said on Tuesday they had advanced to within five km (three miles) of the central Afghan city of Bamiyan, held by a Shi'ite Moslem militia.

Dostum appeared to maintain a shaky grip on the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, but the opposition alliance grouping Dostum with the Shi'ite leader Karim Khalili and former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood seemed in poor shape.

Compared to the strictures imposed in Taleban-held areas, Dostum has maintained a relatively secular social code in cities such as Mazar-i-Sharif, where women can work, girls go to school and even alcohol is not hard to find.
The Taleban Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi on Tuesday reiterated the militia's goal of enforcing strict Islamic Sharia law.

"It is our intention to establish an Islamic government throughout Afghanistan," he told reporters in Kabul. He said an amnesty offered by Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar did not apply to Dostum or former Herat provincial governor Ismail Khan, captured by Malik's men on Monday. They would be tried for their crimes, Mutaqi added.
The Taleban, whose movement emerged less than three years ago from religious schools in Pakistan and southern Afghanistan, may see final victory within their grasp.
But military analysts said the war was not over yet.
"It looks as if the Taleban could march into the north aided by treachery and subterfuge," said one analyst, recalling the militia's past successes in subverting opposing commanders.
"But it's still a very fluid situation," he said. "Malik's men are Uzbeks and have ethnic differences with the Taleban, who are mainly Pashtuns. There may not be much trust between them."
Diplomats said that far from settling the conflict, defeat in the north for Dostum and Masood might simply prompt them to carry on their struggle from outside the country.
"A military takeover by the Taleban does not mean a political solution of the Afghan issue," the U.N. special envoy to Afghanistan, Norbert Holl, told Reuters by telephone.
"I don't think Dostum, Masood or (ousted president Burhanuddin) Rabbani will just give up. I'm sure they will go across the border and establish a government-in-exile."
Some of Afghanistan's neighbours, including mainly Shi'ite Iran and the Central Asian states of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, view the Taleban's Sunni Moslem militancy as a threat.
At a regional summit in the Turkmenistan capital Ashgabat this month, Uzbek President Islam Karimov accused Pakistan of prolonging the Afghan conflict by backing the Taleban.
"It's a tragedy not only for the people of Afghanistan but for the countries neighbouring Afghanistan," he said.

Pakistan has denied supporting the Taleban, saying it has no favourites in Afghanistan, but Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan said during his current visit to Washington that the U.S. government should take a fresh look at the Islamic movement.
He said engagement was the best way to encourage the Taleban to moderate elements of their strict Islamic social code.
Pakistan's friendly relations with the Taleban have strained its ties with Iran, deeply suspicious of a group viewed by the Iranian press as a tool of the United States and Saudi Arabia.

The Taleban have demanded, but so far failed to gain, recognition as the legitimate government of Afghanistan, and have not been able to occupy its seat at the United Nations or other international organisations.
